content: The insecticide Methrin (K-Othrine 250 WDG) is recommended at a target dose of 25 mg of active ingredient (AI) per square meter. Similarly, the organophosphate pirimiphos-methyl (Actellic 300 CS) is used at a target dose of 1 g AI/m², and the carbamate bendiocarb (Ficam 80 WP) is applied at a target dose of 400 mg AI/m². In the case of extending recommendations to broflanilide, a direct entomological comparison was conducted between Vectron™ T500 (target dose: 100 mg AI/m²) and pirimiphos-methyl (Actellic 300 CS). The data from these comparisons were reviewed by WHO technical expert groups, which provided advice to WHO regarding the extension of indoor residual spraying (IRS) recommendations based on their findings. This advice was further evaluated by WHO’s Malaria Policy Advisory Group and, in the case of broflanilide, by the relevant Guideline Development Group (GDG) and the Guideline Review Committee (GRC) secretariat. Comparative efficacy assessments are now integral to the evaluation process for malaria vector control. Any future considerations for extending WHO recommendations for malaria vector control will require, at a minimum, comparative effectiveness data. As of September 2023, WHO has prequalified IRS products from five insecticide classes (pyrethroids, organophosphates, carbamates, neonicotinoids, and broflanilide). However, no organochlorine IRS formulations, including DDT, have been prequalified. Consequently, DDT has not been assessed by WHO for its efficacy, safety, or quality in vector control, and no inspections of manufacturing sites have been conducted. Unlike the other four classes covered by WHO’s IRS recommendations, DDT is classified as a persistent organic pollutant, and its production and use are strictly regulated under the Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants. This international agreement aims to protect human health and the environment from persistent organic pollutants. When the Stockholm Convention was established in 2004, it allowed an exemption for the production and use of DDT for disease vector control due to the lack of equally effective alternatives at the time. However, the recent expansion of IRS products and vector control interventions has provided additional options. WHO actively supports the promotion of chemical safety and, in collaboration with the United Nations Environment Programme, is committed to the global goal of reducing and eventually eliminating the use of DDT while minimizing the burden of vector-borne diseases. The use of DDT for malaria vector control has declined over the years, and WHO supports the continuation of this trend. In certain areas, the use of DDT may still be justified, but such decisions must be based on a detailed analysis of all available vector control options, with clear reasoning for choosing DDT over alternatives. WHO considers DDT a last resort, not a first choice. Proper use and safe storage of DDT require adherence to established national guidelines and WHO technical guidance. Countries using DDT for malaria vector control must reassess its necessity at least every two years and report their findings to the WHO Global Malaria Programme and the Stockholm Convention Secretariat. Continuous use of the same product in the same area over multiple seasons is discouraged, as it may lead to resistance in mosquitoes. Proactive planning for switching to alternative insecticides is essential. Additionally, the residual efficacy of insecticides must be considered, ensuring they remain effective throughout the transmission season when applied to various surfaces (e.g., cement, mud, or wood). Community acceptance of IRS is critical for program success, as it requires householders to permit spray teams to enter their homes and temporarily remove personal items. Some insecticide formulations may leave visible residues or discolor painted surfaces, which can reduce community acceptance. Repeated spraying over extended periods may lead to household refusals, hindering effective IRS implementation. IRS can also be deployed reactively in specific locations where malaria transmission is likely, such as the vicinity of an index case. This approach, known as reactive IRS, is detailed in the WHO guidelines for malaria elimination and prevention of re-establishment. Following insecticide application, it is important to assess the quality of the spraying and monitor residual activity using wall cone bioassays. Entomological surveillance and environmental impact assessments should also be conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of IRS. WHO provides detailed guidance in its operational manual for IRS, which assists malaria program managers, entomologists, and public health officers in designing, implementing, monitoring, and evaluating high-quality IRS programs. A systematic review investigated the impact of residual surface treatment (RST) of insecticides on malaria compared to no vector control intervention. Only studies on IRS were identified, with no studies on outdoor applications or alternative delivery methods. Ten studies from Africa and Asia were included, comprising five cluster-randomized controlled trials (cRCTs), one quasi-experimental study, and four controlled before-and-after studies. The evidence suggested that malaria parasite prevalence was lower in IRS study areas compared to non-IRS areas, but the certainty of evidence was very low. The review excluded studies involving other vector control interventions, such as insecticide-treated nets (ITNs), and did not address comparisons between IRS and ITNs. Subgroup analyses found no significant modifying effects of insecticide class or transmission intensity on malaria incidence and prevalence, but the number of studies was small. The GDG concluded that the impact of IRS likely varies by setting and depends on factors such as malaria transmission intensity, vector behavior, insecticide resistance, IRS coverage, and operational factors. Adverse events associated with IRS were generally mild, such as transient skin irritation and headaches in spray personnel, and were considered small compared to no IRS. The GDG maintained the strong WHO recommendation for IRS based on historical evidence of its impact on malaria control, despite the very low certainty of evidence from the systematic review. WHO encourages further high-quality research to evaluate the impact and potential harms of IRS in various settings, including urbanized areas, alternative delivery methods, and the use of slow-acting insecticides. In humanitarian emergency settings, IRS can be deployed for malaria prevention and control, but its suitability depends on factors such as vector characteristics, human behavior, and infrastructure. Structures must be suitable for spraying, and high coverage must be achievable to provide community-level protection. Emergency settings may pose logistical challenges, such as sourcing commodities and personnel on short notice, which can increase costs. Community acceptance is essential, and messaging may need to be adapted to local languages. WHO recommends using prequalified insecticides and ensuring vector susceptibility to the selected products. Data collection on vector composition, density, behavior, and insecticide susceptibility is crucial for assessing IRS suitability and monitoring its effectiveness.
